Calculate latent VAR impulse response functions

Source: R/irf.mvgam.R
irf.mvgam.Rd

Compute Generalized or Orthogonalized Impulse Response Functions (IRFs) from mvgam models with Vector Autoregressive dynamics. An impulse response traces how the latent trend of every series moves over h time steps after a one-standard-deviation innovation to one series. The default generalised responses suit most analyses. Orthogonalised responses need a causal ordering of the series.

Usage

irf(object, ...)

# S3 method for class 'mvgam'
irf(
  object,
  h = 10,
  cumulative = FALSE,
  orthogonal = FALSE,
  ndraws = NULL,
  draw_ids = NULL,
  summary = TRUE,
  probs = c(0.025, 0.975),
  future = FALSE,
  ...
)

Arguments

object

An object of class mvgam fitted with a VAR() latent process model

...

Unused. Anything passed here is refused.

h

Positive integer. The number of horizons to compute. Horizon 1 is the time step of the shock.

cumulative

Logical. TRUE accumulates each response over the horizons.

orthogonal

Logical. TRUE computes orthogonalised responses from the lower Cholesky factor of the innovation covariance. These depend on the order of the levels of the series factor. The default generalised responses do not (Pesaran and Shin 1998).

ndraws

Positive integer specifying number of posterior draws to use. NULL (default) uses all available draws.

draw_ids

Optional integer vector selecting a subset of posterior draw indices to use. NULL (default) uses all draws (subject to ndraws).

summary

Logical; return the posterior median and interval of each response (the default), or the per-draw responses themselves. The draws are one K by K matrix per horizon per draw, which on a wide panel runs to hundreds of megabytes.

probs

The lower and upper percentiles of the interval reported with the median when summary = TRUE.

future

Logical. When TRUE, the per-draw computation runs under the future::plan() the caller has set. The default sequential plan runs as base lapply() does. plan(multisession, workers = N) splits the draws across N R processes. Without the future package the draws run in turn, with a message.

Value

An object of mvgam_irf-class. plot.mvgam_irf() and summary.mvgam_irf() take it.

Details

See mvgam_irf-class for the quantities computed and returned, with references.

References

Lutkepohl H (2005). New Introduction to Multiple Time Series Analysis. Springer, Berlin. doi:10.1007/978-3-540-27752-1

Pesaran HH and Shin Y (1998). Generalized impulse response analysis in linear multivariate models. Economics Letters 58, 17-29. doi:10.1016/S0165-1765(97)00214-0

See also

fevd() and stability() summarise the same VAR dynamics. The VAR article runs irf() on a plankton community. The hierarchical VAR article runs it on each group of a hierarchical VAR.

Other latent dynamics: active_factors(), compare_loadings(), fevd.mvgam(), ordinate(), posterior_transition_matrix(), residual_cor(), shared_variation(), stability.mvgam()

Author

Nicholas J Clark

Examples

# \dontrun{
set.seed(0)
simdat <- sim_mvgam(family = gaussian(), n_series = 3L,
                    n_timepoints = 120L, trend_model = VAR(),
                    prop_trend = 0.95)
var_mod <- mvgam(y ~ 1, trend_formula = ~ VAR(p = 1),
                 data = simdat$data_train, family = gaussian(),
                 chains = 2, silent = 2)
#> Warning: 44 of 2000 (2.0%) transitions ended with a divergence.
#> See https://mc-stan.org/misc/warnings for details.
#> Warning: 1 of 2 chains had an E-BFMI less than 0.3.
#> See https://mc-stan.org/misc/warnings for details.

# Generalised responses of every series to a shock in each
irf_obj <- irf(var_mod, h = 8L)
plot(irf_obj, series = 1)


# Next: fevd() splits each series' forecast variance among the
# shocks. stability() summarises how the system returns to
# equilibrium
# }
